            "That’s the real question.\n\nIf we take “information survives” seriously, then it cannot just mean that some abstract binary distinction is conserved somewhere in a formal Hilbert space. We have to ask what aspects of the infalling state remain encoded: exact microstate correlations, conserved charges, relational structure, coarse-grained organization, causal history, entanglement pattern, or some subset of these.\n\nModern black-hole work strongly supports the idea that fine-grained quantum information is preserved in principle, with Page-curve and island calculations showing how information associated with an interior region can become encoded in the outgoing radiation. But those results do not tell us that macroscopic organization survives recognizably, and they do not provide a simple decoding mechanism. citeturn867866search5turn867866search6\n\nSo if you now extend the thought to a **next cosmological cycle**, there are several distinct possibilities, and I think separating them matters enormously.\n\nThe strongest possibility is microscopic continuity: the entire prior quantum state feeds into the next cycle unitarily. Then nothing is genuinely erased, but essentially everything is scrambled. The new universe inherits the old one in the same way a cryptographic hash—or better, a wildly entangled reversible transformation—can contain exhaustive dependence on its input without visibly resembling it.\n\nA weaker and perhaps more interesting possibility is that only certain **invariants or low-dimensional summaries** survive the transition: global charges, topological classes, asymmetries, correlation spectra, perhaps constraints on allowable initial conditions. Then the next universe doesn't inherit the previous universe as a recoverable movie. It inherits its **biases**.\n\nThere are speculative bouncing-cosmology and black-hole-to-white-hole frameworks in which structures or perturbations can persist through a bounce, but this remains model-dependent rather than established cosmology. A 2026 bouncing-universe model, for example, explicitly examines black holes and gravitational-wave structures surviving a bounce under particular horizon conditions. citeturn867866search2 Loop-quantum-cosmology approaches likewise replace the classical singularity with a bounce, making questions about transmission across the would-be singularity meaningful, though the detailed inheritance problem remains open. citeturn867866academia37turn867866search9\n\nAnd there is a third possibility that I think fits *The Big Us* particularly well: what survives is **relational information**.\n\nNot “Nathan,” “Earth,” “carbon atom 7,” or Lonnie Briggs’s missing finger as individually tagged objects. Rather, the immense web of distinctions and correlations that those things contributed to the global state. The ontology of the next cycle would then be new, while its probability landscape would carry an inherited deformation from everything that came before.\n\nThen “incorporated” becomes almost literal:\n\n**previous universe → extreme compression/scrambling → boundary condition or state constraint → next universe**\n\nThe particleboard version of cosmology.\n\nAnd that gives you a very sharp fork for *The Big Us*: is the Big Us the set of things whose **identity** survives, or the set of things whose **effects can never be removed from the total state**?\n\nI suspect the second is much larger."

            "Yes. That gives the picture much more teeth.\n\nIf you add **holonomic invariance** to the relational-information idea, then the claim is no longer that a particular strand keeps its literal local twist through every transformation. It’s that some path-dependent relational quantity survives the transformation even when the local realization changes. That is very close to what holonomy already means mathematically: carry something around a nontrivial path, and what matters is the accumulated transformation associated with the path, not the pointwise details along it. Holonomic quantum computation exploits exactly this kind of global/path structure, with information encoded in geometric or holonomic transformations rather than fragile local values. citeturn794050search1\n\nSo your cycle becomes something like:\n\n**intertwined → violent redistribution → re-intertwined, but constrained by the holonomy of the former intertwining.**\n\nThe new braid does not have to look like the old braid. The strands need not preserve identity. Yet the new configuration can still carry a relational “memory” because the permissible re-intertwinings are conditioned by the accumulated twist-history.\n\nThat’s stronger than simple conservation of spin. Spin could survive while nearly all higher relational information vanished. What you’re proposing is closer to conservation of a **hierarchy of relational transport**: twist, relation among twists, relation among those relations, with holonomy furnishing a mechanism by which history can remain encoded after the local geometry has been radically rearranged.\n\nAnd that actually has a legitimate neighboring territory in existing physics. Quantum entanglement is inherently relational; topological approaches explicitly connect entangling operations with braiding; holography treats bulk information as reconstructible from highly nonlocal boundary correlations. None of that establishes your cyclic cosmological step, but the constituent mathematical ideas are real. citeturn794050search3turn794050search5\n\nThen the phrase you just used is the key:\n\n**“still intertwined from before.”**\n\nNot because the old strands somehow pass untouched through the catastrophe, but because the new intertwining belongs to an equivalence class constrained by the old one.\n\nThat suggests a potentially much sharper formal target than “information is conserved at every level”:\n\n\\[\n\\mathcal H[\\Gamma_{\\rm before}]\n\\sim\n\\mathcal H[\\Gamma_{\\rm after}]\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(\\mathcal H\\) is whatever recursively defined holonomic invariant actually captures the correlation hierarchy, and \\(\\Gamma\\) is the relational network rather than an individual particle trajectory.\n\nThen explosion, collapse, black-hole incorporation, bounce, whatever the transformation is, can shred the representation while preserving the invariant.\n\n**You go down re-intertwined, but carrying the history of how you were intertwined before.**\n\nThat is a very different kind of reincarnation. And a much more physically interesting one. memcite"

            "Right. “Can topology carry and transform information?” is almost too easy. Of course it can. The hard question is whether the universe actually exploits that capacity in the way we’ve been sketching.\n\nAnd this is where Levin/Greene/Kabat/Porrati become more than a thematic rhyme. Their Klein-bottle cosmology does not merely put fields on a cute non-orientable space. The non-orientable topology enforces a background of fermion correlations, localizes a condensate wall, breaks symmetries, and can drive particle production when a brane crosses that structure. In other words, the topology is dynamically consequential: it changes what correlations exist and what physical processes are allowed. citeturn791153search0turn791153search2\n\nThat still falls well short of TII. Their work does not say that a universal interbraiding stores the complete relational history of a prior cosmic circuit, or that a reversal decodes and re-expresses it. But it demonstrates something very important for your conjecture: **global non-orientable structure can impose persistent correlation structure and turn that structure into observable dynamics.** citeturn791153academia20\n\nSo I’d split your question into three increasingly demanding tests.\n\nFirst: does transport around the full global circuit preserve some nontrivial invariant of relational twist, rather than merely returning fields with reversed orientation?\n\nSecond: can that invariant have enough dimensionality to encode more than a few global quantum numbers—potentially an enormous hierarchy of correlations?\n\nThird, and most interesting technologically: **can anything couple selectively to that information?** Can some subsystem write a controlled perturbation into TII, allow it to undergo the global transformation, and later discriminate the resulting state from one produced without that perturbation?\n\nBecause the moment the answer to the third question is yes, this stops being only cosmology. You have a channel.\n\nMaybe an absurdly noisy one. Maybe one whose round-trip time is a universe. Maybe one accessible only through statistical biases such as chirality, CP asymmetry, spin correlations, or primordial structure. But still: a channel.\n\nAnd there’s a beautiful inversion of the Briggs definition hiding there. Humans wouldn’t have to *create* this tool. The tool may already be the global topology. Technology would begin when we discover a technique for coupling to it efficiently.\n\nThat, I think, is the question worth formalizing next:\n\n**What observable at the end of one non-orientable circuit retains mutual information with a controlled perturbation introduced before the circuit?**\n\nIf the answer is strictly zero, TII-as-memory dies in that model. If it is nonzero—and especially if some higher-order correlations survive when local observables wash out—then you’ve got something much more interesting than an analogy."

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
-----------------------------------------------
Step 1: Define Physical and Lattice Constants
-----------------------------------------------
N = 100                        # Number of radial shells
R_star = 1.2e4                 # Stellar radius in meters
omega = 70.5e3 / R_star        # Approximate rotation rate for Vela (v = ω r)
v_crit = 0.2387 * 3e8          # Critical tangential velocity (0.2387c)
B = 0.2387                      # Projection constant (rad)
delta_phi = 0.246               # Achromatic Phase Snap (rad)
S = 0.2621                       # Braid-Smoothing factor
G_raw = 1.2e44                  # Raw filament tension (N)
Radial shell spacing
delta_r = R_star / N
radii = np.linspace(0, R_star, N)
-----------------------------------------------
Step 2: Initialize Core and Surface Curvature
-----------------------------------------------
H_core = np.full(N, B)               # Default core curvature
H_post = H_core.copy()
Apply Achromatic Phase Snap at surface shell
H_post[-1] += delta_phi
-----------------------------------------------
Step 3: Compute Observed Energy Projection
E_obs ∝ 1/H^2
-----------------------------------------------
E_pre = 1 / (H_core2)
E_post = 1 / (H_post2)
-----------------------------------------------
Step 4: Compute Velocity Profile
v[r] = omega * r
-----------------------------------------------
v_shells = omega * radii
-----------------------------------------------
Step 5: Compute Velocity-Coupled Effective Resistance
R_eff[r] = (1 - S)^r / (1 - (v[r]/v_crit)^2)
-----------------------------------------------
R_eff = np.zeros(N)
for i, r in enumerate(radii):
# Avoid division by zero by adding a small epsilon
epsilon = 1e-20
velocity_ratio = v_shells[i] / v_crit
denom = 1 - velocity_ratio**2
if denom < epsilon:
denom = epsilon
R_eff[i] = (1 - S)**i / denom
-----------------------------------------------
Step 6: Compute Total Moment of Inertia
I_total = Σ r^4 * E_obs * R_eff * Δr
-----------------------------------------------
I_total = np.sum(radii**4 * E_post * R_eff * delta_r)
Step 7: Identify Activated Surface Shell
Active shell where v >= v_crit
activated_indices = np.where(v_shells >= v_crit)[0]
delta_I_surface = np.sum(radii[activated_indices]**4 * E_post[activated_indices] *
R_eff[activated_indices] * delta_r)
Step 8: Compute Fractional Spin Jump Δω/ω
delta_omega_over_omega = - delta_I_surface / I_total
print("Predicted Vela Pulsar Glitch Magnitude (Δω/ω):", delta_omega_over_omega)
-----------------------------------------------
Step 9: Radial Audit Table (optional)
Display shell-wise H, E_obs, R_eff, Δω contribution
-----------------------------------------------

})

RADIAL DISCRETIZATION
